Buffon's Needle

ProbabilityAreaLimits
Game: This shows what happens when a needle, or a bent noodle of the same length, is thrown over and over onto a floor with evenly spaced cracks.
How to play: Press Start to throw needles and watch the count, then draw a noodle and save it to see if the answer changes.

Crossings / throws: 0 / 0

Drag on the pad to place the corners of a broken line, or focus it and press Enter for each corner. Press Save noodle when it looks right.

Look for the math

A needle dropped on a ruled floor can tell you something about π. The surprise is that the needle need not be straight: a bent wire of the same length gives the same answer.

The chance of crossing a crack

The floor here has two cracks, exactly one needle-length apart. The needle's middle lands equally anywhere between them, and it points in any direction with equal chance. It crosses a crack when its low end reaches the lower crack or its high end reaches the upper one. Working that out gives a chance of 2L / (π D), and since here L = D, the chance is just 2 / π, about 0.637. This is the first problem of geometric probability. The logic test checks the formula by trying every angle and position on a fine grid, and confirms the value 2/π.

Why the shape does not matter

Think of a bent noodle as many short straight needles joined end to end. Each short piece has the same chance of crossing as any other piece of its length, no matter which way it points or where it hangs. The expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, so the whole noodle's expected crossings depend only on its total length. The test confirms this for a straight needle, a right angle, a zigzag and an arc: all four give 2/π crossings per throw. Because a noodle can cross a crack more than once in one throw, the count on the floor is the number of crossings, not the number of throws that crossed.

Turning counts into π

If T throws make C crossings, then C / T is about 2 / π, so π ≈ 2T / C. The reading in the corner shows C / T; tick Show π estimate to see the second number too, cut short to six characters just as the old applet did (the original page left this option off). A longer run steadies the answer: the test uses 200,000 throws and lands close to 3.14159. The page's claim that Buffon posed the first problem of geometric probability in the 18th century is history, not a formula we can check here.

Try saving a wild zigzag and a nearly straight noodle. Can you tell their crossing counts apart after only 500 throws? What about after 10,000?
